ELUCIDATION
OF
REGIONAL REGULATION OF PEKALONGAN CITY
NUMBER 5 OF 2015
CONCERNING
THE IMPLEMENTATION OF PROTECTION FOR
VICTIMS OF GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE AND CHILDREN

I. GENERAL

The State has an obligation to provide a sense of security to its citizens from threats and actions that can disturb and damage psychological, physical, sexual and economic security. This is philosophically stated in the preamble of the 1945 Constitution, that the purpose of establishing the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia is to protect the entire Nation and the Homeland of Indonesia. Because the Government of Indonesia has signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR 1948) and ratified CEDAW (Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women), it is obligated to fulfill these provisions.

Human Rights state that the enforcement and fulfillment of Human Rights is the responsibility of the State, especially the Government. Through Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, the government recognizes the existence of children's rights. The inherent human rights of children include basic rights as human beings, namely the Right to Life, the Right to Growth and Development, the Right to Protection and the Right to Participation. To fulfill the Right to life, children need food in sufficient quantities, healthy and nutritious, as well as optimal health access. Protection from violence that threatens their safety and health must be provided from an early age. Protection is needed to prevent physical, mental and sexual violence and exploitation. To fulfill the right to growth and development, children need space to play, exercise, and education that is appropriate to their physical and psychological development.

In fulfilling children's rights, every government administrator, community and parents are obligated to understand and care about children's rights. The existence of legal instruments and law enforcement officials who defend the interests of children is necessary for this protection effort. Legislation that is principled on defending the best interest of the child is needed to realize protection that is legal in nature. Furthermore, it is not uncommon to find cases of women and children who experience problems of physical, psychological, sexual and social violence. For example, women and children who are victims of persecution, neglect, eviction and abuse by parents or others. For women and children who experience these problems, the government must provide a Safe House (children protection home) or Integrated Service Center (PPT) for women and children victims of violence. The Safe House or PPT is a safe place and is friendly in nature for women and children. The PPT is equipped with companions from educators, doctors, psychologists, religious leaders and networked with lawyers for women and children as well as the RPK Unit at the Police.

The fate of women and children victims of violence must be given attention by the government. The large number of cases of violence against women and children are often caused by factors that develop in society, for example low levels of economy, education, and environments located in the industrial sector. Therefore, victims of violence like this need to receive protection in accordance with the principles of justice, truth, legal certainty, equality and upholding human rights. For the empowerment of victims of violence, local governments can establish an Integrated Service Center for the Empowerment of Women and Children (P2TP2A) as a center for empowering women victims of violence which specifically has the main duties and functions for empowerment of women and children victims of violence. From the framework above, the Government is responsible for taking actions both legally, politically, economically and socially to prevent, suppress, reduce, and eliminate all forms of violence against women and children. From these various efforts, a legal framework will be realized in the implementation of protection for victims of gender-based violence and children.

Article 16
In addition to victims of gender-based violence and children, the forms of services and assistance organized by LP-PAR are also provided to Children in Conflict with the Law. In legal literature, ABH states that Children in conflict with the law are children who have reached the age of 12 (twelve) years but have not reached the age of 18 (eighteen) years and are not yet married:
a. Who are suspected, alleged, accused, or sentenced for committing a criminal offense;
b. Who become victims of a criminal offense or who see and/or hear directly the occurrence of a criminal offense.
Children in conflict with the law can also be defined as children who are forced to come into contact with the criminal justice system because:
a. They are suspected, accused, or declared proven guilty of violating the law
b. They have become victims as a result of acts of legal violations committed by a person/group of persons/institution/state against them; or
c. They have seen, heard, felt, or known of an incident of legal violation.
There are two categories of child behavior that cause them to come into conflict with the law:
a. Status Offence, namely delinquent behavior of children which if committed by adults is not considered a crime, for example: skipping school, running away from home, etc.
b. Juvenile Delinquency, namely delinquent behavior of children which if committed by adults is considered a crime or criminal act, for example: robbery, rape, sexual harassment, etc. Therefore, if viewed from its scope, children in conflict with the law can be divided into:
a. Perpetrators or suspects of criminal offenses;
b. Victims of criminal offenses;
c. Witnesses to a criminal offense As a child, the legal mechanism and sense of justice in society must be placed within a framework that constructively encourages their physical and psychological development.
The forms of services and assistance organized by LP-PAR are also provided to women in conflict with the law.
Legal protection of women's interests in performing their position in society requires the preparation of various laws and regulations, and the consistent enforcement thereof, as well as socialization activities to raise awareness of their rights and obligations. In addition, non-legal support is needed, because law is only one means of social control. Action agendas from various components of society in an integrative manner need and must be immediately realized.
Furthermore, in the context of empowerment and protection of women, there needs to be legal, psychological, social and economic assistance when women are faced with legal processes.

Article 11
In order to provide services and protection against gender-based and child violence, the Regional Government establishes the Women, Children and Adolescent Protection Institution (LP PAR) as an integrated service center for victims of gender-based and child violence.

Sixth Part

12. Gender-Based Violence is any form of restriction, exclusion, differentiation and all forms of treatment carried out on the basis of gender and aimed at reducing, eliminating the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights, the consequences of which include and are not limited to physical, sexual, psychological and economic violence.

15. Physical violence is any act that results in pain, injury, wounds or defects on a person's body, miscarriage or fainting and/or causes death.

17. Sexual violence is any act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, whether unnatural or unwanted with another person for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes.
18. Victims of acts of violence are individuals or groups of people who experience physical, mental or emotional suffering, economic loss, or experience neglect, reduction or deprivation of their basic rights, as a result of human rights (HAM) violations, or criminal acts as well as acts of violence committed either by state apparatus or by the state or regional government apparatus or by individuals.

Article 7
(1) The obligations and responsibilities of the Regional Government as referred to in Article 6 letter a, include:
a. implementing protection policies against gender-based violence and violence against children established by the government; b. establishing policies, programs, and activities for protection against gender-based violence and violence against children; c. conducting cooperation in the implementation of protection for women and children from acts of violence;
d. providing support for facilities and infrastructure for the implementation of protection against gender-based violence and violence against children;
e. allocating budget for the implementation of protection against gender-based violence and violence against children in accordance with regional financial capacity; and
f. fostering and supervising the implementation of protection against gender-based violence and violence against children. (2) In order to carry out the obligations and responsibilities as referred to in paragraph (1), the regional government establishes action programs and activities for the protection of gender and children in 1 (one) Regional Action Plan as a basis for SKPD in implementing protection against gender-based violence and violence against children.

Part Eight
Empowerment of Victims of Acts of Violence

3.2.rationale: In the Indonesian source, the regulation establishes an integrated service institution (LP PAR) (Pasal 11) and defines “Perlindungan” as efforts that can be carried out by various parties including “kepolisian” (Pasal 1 angka 9). The Elucidation (Penjelasan Umum) mentions the PPT being “berjaringan dengan ... Unit RPK di Kepolisian” (networked with the RPK unit at the police). However, nowhere does the Perda create/mandate a specialised police service unit within police offices; it only references coordination/networking with an existing police unit. Therefore a “Yes” for an indicator requiring a specialised police unit is not supported by the Indonesian text; the judge’s ‘No’ is consistent, suggesting the golden label is likely incorrect.

This matches the English candidate passage and supports a ‘Yes’ if the indicator is about addressing women’s involvement in legal processes (as victims/accused/witnesses) via services/assistance. Since the judge relied on accurate content and reasoning, the golden label ‘No’ appears inconsistent with the Indonesian text.
